title: B1 Consolidation
subtitle: Tell a complete story, debate with structure, and write letters in any register

lessons.title: Récit complet
lessons.description: Combine imparfait, passé composé, and plus-que-parfait into one flowing narrative.

blocks.heading: Trois temps, une histoire
blocks.body: A rich story layers three past tenses. The imparfait paints the background — what things were like. The passé composé reports what happened — the events that move the plot. The plus-que-parfait reaches further back, for something that had already happened before the main story started. Together they give a story real depth.

examples.french: Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti de la gare.
examples.english: It was raining when I left the station.

examples.french: J'ai reconnu tout de suite la maison.
examples.english: I immediately recognized the house.

examples.french: J'y avais passé toutes mes vacances d'enfance.
examples.english: I had spent all my childhood holidays there.

examples.french: Elle avait déjà fermé la porte quand j'ai crié.
examples.english: She had already closed the door by the time I shouted.

blocks.tip: Ask three questions in order: what was the scene (imparfait)? What happened (passé composé)? What had already happened before that (plus-que-parfait)?

blocks.heading: Organiser le récit dans le temps
blocks.body: Time connectors keep a long story easy to follow. D'abord, puis, and enfin mark the main steps. La veille and le lendemain jump a day back or forward without changing tense. Auparavant signals something further in the past, often paired with the plus-que-parfait.

examples.french: D'abord, nous avons pris le train jusqu'à Lyon.
examples.english: First, we took the train to Lyon.

examples.french: La veille, j'avais préparé mon sac en vitesse.
examples.english: The day before, I'd packed my bag in a hurry.

examples.french: Puis, nous avons marché deux heures sous la pluie.
examples.english: Then, we walked two hours in the rain.

examples.french: Auparavant, je n'étais jamais parti seul.
examples.english: Before that, I'd never traveled alone.

examples.french: Le lendemain, tout allait déjà mieux.
examples.english: The next day, everything was already better.

blocks.heading: Ajouter du relief
blocks.body: A flat list of events isn't a story. Soudain and tout à coup break the rhythm to signal a surprise. En fait corrects what the listener assumed. Quand même shows something happened despite the odds. A well-placed rebondissement (plot twist) is what makes people want to hear the end.

examples.french: Soudain, je me suis rendu compte que j'avais oublié mon passeport.
examples.english: Suddenly, I realized I'd forgotten my passport.

examples.french: En fait, ce n'était pas la bonne adresse.
examples.english: Actually, it wasn't the right address.

examples.french: On a raté le dernier bus, mais on est arrivés à temps quand même.
examples.english: We missed the last bus, but we still arrived on time.

examples.french: Et là, tout à coup, un vrai rebondissement : elle nous attendait déjà sur le quai.
examples.english: And then, all of a sudden, a real plot twist: she was already waiting for us on the platform.

blocks.tip: Save your best rebondissement for last — French listeners love a story that ends on a twist, signaled by "et là..." (and then...).

items.exampleEnglish: All of that happened in a single night.

items.example: On a fini par retrouver notre chemin.

items.exampleEnglish: After two hours, someone finally came.

blocks.heading: Le plus-que-parfait dans le récit
blocks.body: The plus-que-parfait (avais/avait + past participle) narrates something that had already happened before the main story's timeline. It lets you explain a cause, a flashback, or context the reader needs before the action continues. It always looks back from a point that is already in the past.

examples.french: Quand je suis arrivé, elle était déjà partie.
examples.english: When I arrived, she had already left.

examples.french: Il avait plu toute la nuit, alors les routes étaient glissantes.
examples.english: It had rained all night, so the roads were slippery.

examples.french: Nous n'avions jamais vu une tempête pareille avant ce jour-là.
examples.english: We had never seen such a storm before that day.

examples.french: J'ai compris pourquoi : ils avaient changé d'horaire sans nous prévenir.
examples.english: I understood why: they had changed the schedule without telling us.

blocks.tip: If you can insert "already" or "by then" naturally in English, French almost certainly needs the plus-que-parfait.

blocks.heading: Choisir le bon temps, phrase par phrase
blocks.body: Before each sentence in a story, decide: is this the backdrop (imparfait), the next event (passé composé), or something earlier still (plus-que-parfait)? A single paragraph often needs all three, moving smoothly between them as the story layers past-within-past.

examples.french: Il faisait froid ce soir-là. (imparfait)
examples.english: It was cold that evening.

examples.french: Nous avons décidé de rentrer plus tôt. (passé composé)
examples.english: We decided to go home earlier.

examples.french: Nous avions déjà annulé nos autres projets. (plus-que-parfait)
examples.english: We had already canceled our other plans.

examples.french: Alors la soirée s'est terminée en douceur. (passé composé)
examples.english: So the evening ended gently.

blocks.tip: Read your story aloud tense by tense — if the order of events feels confusing, you probably need a plus-que-parfait somewhere.

passages.title: Le train de nuit
passages.french:
L'an dernier, j'ai vécu une aventure que je raconte encore à tout le monde.
Ce soir-là, je devais prendre le dernier train pour rentrer chez moi.
Auparavant, j'avais réservé ma place sans faire attention à l'horaire.
Quand je suis arrivé sur le quai, le train était déjà parti depuis dix minutes.
J'étais furieux contre moi-même : j'avais mal lu le billet.
Soudain, une employée m'a proposé une solution à laquelle je n'avais pas pensé.
Elle m'a expliqué qu'un autre train partait une heure plus tard, en direction de la même ville.
Entre-temps, je me suis assis sur un banc et j'ai appelé ma sœur pour la prévenir.
Au fur et à mesure que le temps passait, mon inquiétude a peu à peu disparu.
Finalement, je suis monté dans ce train de remplacement, presque vide et silencieux.
Le lendemain matin, je me suis rendu compte que j'avais adoré ce voyage imprévu.
Bref, ce petit rebondissement est devenu mon meilleur souvenir de l'année.
passages.english:
Last year, I lived through an adventure that I still tell everyone about.
That evening, I was supposed to catch the last train home.
Beforehand, I had booked my seat without paying attention to the schedule.
When I arrived on the platform, the train had already left ten minutes earlier.
I was furious with myself: I had misread the ticket.
Suddenly, an employee offered me a solution I hadn't thought of.
She explained that another train was leaving an hour later, heading to the same city.
Meanwhile, I sat down on a bench and called my sister to let her know.
As time went by, my worry gradually disappeared.
In the end, I got on this replacement train, almost empty and silent.
The next morning, I realized I had loved this unplanned trip.
In short, this little plot twist became my best memory of the year.

lessons.title: Débat structuré
lessons.description: Present an opinion, concede a point, and conclude a structured argument.

blocks.heading: Présenter son opinion clairement
blocks.body: A structured debate opens with a clear stance. À mon avis, d'après moi, and personnellement all introduce a personal opinion — use one, not all three, to avoid sounding repetitive. Franchement adds honesty, and reconnaître que lets you name a fact before arguing your point.

examples.french: À mon avis, cette mesure est nécessaire.
examples.english: In my opinion, this measure is necessary.

examples.french: D'après moi, le débat est mal posé.
examples.english: In my view, the debate is framed wrong.

examples.french: Personnellement, je reste sceptique.
examples.english: Personally, I remain skeptical.

examples.french: Je reconnais que le sujet est complexe, mais...
examples.english: I admit the subject is complex, but...

blocks.tip: Open with your opinion, not a question — French debate style states a position first, then defends it.

blocks.heading: Concéder un point
blocks.body: A convincing debater doesn't ignore the other side — they concede a point, then pivot back to their own argument. Bien que and même si (+ subjunctive with bien que) introduce the opponent's valid point; cependant, toutefois, en revanche, and néanmoins pivot back. Malgré tout keeps your conclusion standing despite the concession.

examples.french: Bien que je comprenne cet avis, je ne le partage pas.
examples.english: Although I understand that view, I don't share it.

examples.french: Il est vrai que le prix a augmenté ; cependant, la qualité aussi.
examples.english: It's true the price went up; however, so did the quality.

examples.french: Certes, il y a des risques ; toutefois, les bénéfices sont plus grands.
examples.english: Granted, there are risks; nevertheless, the benefits are greater.

examples.french: Malgré tout, je maintiens ma position.
examples.english: Despite all that, I stand by my position.

blocks.tip: Bien que always takes the subjunctive: "bien que ce soit difficile", not "bien que c'est difficile".

blocks.heading: Conclure un débat
blocks.body: A structured argument ends with a clear synthesis, not a new point. En conclusion and pour conclure formally announce the wrap-up. En somme and bref summarize more casually. Repeat your central argument in one short sentence so the listener remembers exactly what you defended.

examples.french: En conclusion, cette réforme mérite d'être testée.
examples.english: In conclusion, this reform deserves to be tested.

examples.french: Pour conclure, je pense que le débat doit continuer.
examples.english: To conclude, I think the debate must continue.

examples.french: En somme, les deux points de vue se valent.
examples.english: All in all, both points of view are equally valid.

examples.french: Bref, rien n'est encore décidé.
examples.english: In short, nothing is decided yet.

blocks.tip: A strong conclusion is one sentence long — resist the urge to add a brand-new argument at the very end.

blocks.heading: Le subjonctif après bien que et les expressions de doute
blocks.body: Bien que always triggers the subjunctive, because a concession is a subjective, not a factual, statement. The same pattern applies after expressions of doubt (je doute que, il n'est pas certain que) that you'll often use when weighing an opponent's argument. Facts, on the other hand (il est vrai que, je pense que in the affirmative), stay in the indicative.

examples.french: Bien que l'idée soit intéressante, elle reste risquée.
examples.english: Although the idea is interesting, it remains risky.

examples.french: Je doute que cette solution suffise.
examples.english: I doubt this solution will be enough.

examples.french: Il n'est pas certain que tout le monde soit d'accord.
examples.english: It's not certain that everyone will agree.

examples.french: Je pense que ce choix est raisonnable. (indicative — certainty)
examples.english: I think this choice is reasonable.

blocks.tip: Doubt and concession live in the subjunctive; certainty and fact live in the indicative — ask yourself which one you're expressing.

blocks.heading: Structurer un argument en trois temps
blocks.body: A B1 argument follows a simple, reusable shape: state your opinion, concede a counterpoint, then conclude. Linking words carry the structure so the listener never gets lost: à mon avis / il est vrai que ... cependant ... en conclusion. Reusing this three-part skeleton works for almost any debate topic.

examples.french: À mon avis, il faut agir vite.
examples.english: In my opinion, we need to act quickly.

examples.french: Il est vrai que ce changement demande du temps.
examples.english: It's true that this change takes time.

examples.french: Cependant, attendre coûterait bien plus cher.
examples.english: However, waiting would cost far more.

examples.french: En conclusion, je pense qu'il faut commencer dès maintenant.
examples.english: In conclusion, I think we should start right now.

blocks.tip: Practice the skeleton with a neutral topic first (le télétravail, les réseaux sociaux) before applying it to a subject you feel strongly about.

passages.title: Faut-il interdire les téléphones au collège ?
passages.french:
À mon avis, interdire les téléphones au collège est une bonne décision.
D'après moi, les élèves se concentrent mieux quand l'écran n'est pas à portée de main.
Selon une étude récente, les résultats scolaires s'améliorent nettement après une interdiction.
Il est vrai que le téléphone peut aussi servir pour les cours, certains professeurs l'utilisent.
Cependant, dans la pratique, la plupart des élèves l'utilisent surtout pour discuter entre eux.
Certes, une interdiction totale semble sévère, mais elle a le mérite d'être simple à appliquer.
En revanche, il faudrait prévoir une exception pour les urgences familiales.
D'une part, les parents s'inquiètent de ne plus pouvoir joindre leurs enfants.
D'autre part, un téléphone à l'accueil du collège pourrait régler ce problème facilement.
Malgré tout, je reconnais que certains élèves plus âgés géreraient très bien la liberté du portable.
En conclusion, je soutiens une interdiction, mais avec un peu de souplesse pour les cas particuliers.

lessons.title: Écrire une lettre
lessons.description: Write a formal letter and an informal message side by side, reviewing register throughout.

blocks.heading: Choisir le bon registre
blocks.body: Every piece of writing has a register: formel for strangers, institutions, and professional contacts; informel for friends and family. The registre shows in your choice of vous vs tu, your vocabulary, and your opening and closing lines. Reading the situation correctly is the whole skill — the grammar itself rarely changes.

examples.french: On vouvoie toujours dans une lettre formelle.
examples.english: You always use "vous" in a formal letter.

examples.french: Entre amis, on tutoie et on reste informel.
examples.english: Between friends, you use "tu" and stay informal.

examples.french: Il faut respecter les convenances avec un inconnu.
examples.english: You need to respect social conventions with a stranger.

examples.french: Le registre change tout, même si le message est le même.
examples.english: Register changes everything, even when the message is the same.

blocks.tip: When in doubt about register, formal is always the safer default — you can always relax it later if invited to.

blocks.heading: La lettre formelle
blocks.body: A formal French letter follows a fixed skeleton: Madame, Monsieur (if you don't know the name), then l'objet in one line, the body in short clear paragraphs, and a closing formula like veuillez agréer... or the shorter cordialement. Anything you attach is announced with ci-joint or vous trouverez en pièce jointe.

examples.french: Madame, Monsieur,
examples.english: Dear Sir or Madam,

examples.french: Objet : demande de renseignements
examples.english: Subject: request for information

examples.french: Vous trouverez ci-joint une copie de mon dossier.
examples.english: Please find enclosed a copy of my file.

examples.french: Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées.
examples.english: Please accept, Sir or Madam, my distinguished regards.

blocks.tip: "Cordialement" alone is a modern, safe closing for professional email — it's less stiff than the full "veuillez agréer" formula.

blocks.heading: Le message informel
blocks.body: An informal message drops the fixed skeleton entirely. Salut or Coucou replaces Madame, Monsieur. Sentences get shorter, contractions appear (t'as, j'sais pas), and the closing becomes warm and personal: bises, à bientôt, or grosses bises for close friends and family.

examples.french: Salut ! Ça va ?
examples.english: Hi! How are you?

examples.french: Bref, je te raconterai tout ça de vive voix.
examples.english: Anyway, I'll tell you all about it in person.

examples.french: À bientôt !
examples.english: See you soon!

examples.french: Bises, Léa
examples.english: Kisses, Léa

blocks.tip: The same request ("can you send me the document?") sounds completely different formal vs informal — compare "pourriez-vous m'envoyer..." to "tu peux m'envoyer...".

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel de politesse
blocks.body: Formal requests almost always use the conditional, not the present tense — it softens a demand into a polite suggestion. Je souhaiterais, je voudrais, pourriez-vous, and auriez-vous l'amabilité de all belong to this register and pair naturally with vouvoyer.

examples.english: I would like to get an appointment.

examples.french: Pourriez-vous me confirmer la date ?
examples.english: Could you confirm the date for me?

examples.english: Would you be so kind as to reply quickly?

examples.french: J'aimerais avoir davantage de précisions.
examples.english: I would like to have more details.

blocks.tip: Compare the register jump: "Envoie-moi le fichier" (informal, present) vs "Pourriez-vous m'envoyer le fichier ?" (formal, conditional).

blocks.heading: Deux lettres, deux structures
blocks.body: Formal and informal writing follow different skeletons, not just different vocabulary. Formal: Madame/Monsieur → objet → corps clair → formule de politesse. Informal: Salut/Coucou → message libre, souvent avec des phrases courtes → bises/à bientôt. Knowing both skeletons by heart lets you write confidently in either register at any moment.
